content: The Pan-African Rabies Control Network (PARACON) was established by merging the Southern and Eastern African Rabies Group with the African Rabies Expert Bureau. This initiative expanded to include African countries not previously associated with either organization. Through workshops organized by PARACON and other regional networks, the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC) and international partners utilize tools like the Rabies Blueprint and the Stepwise Approach to Rabies Elimination (SARE) to assist countries in advancing toward the elimination of dog-mediated rabies. A new epidemiological bulletin from PARACON aims to enhance the collection and visibility of surveillance data critical for monitoring rabies control progress. In Latin America, the Regional Program for Rabies Control (REDIPRA) convenes biennially to evaluate rabies control strategies, provide recommendations to countries, and coordinate regional responses. The 15th REDIPRA meeting, held in Brazil in 2015, emphasized the importance of surveillance in the remaining areas where dog-mediated rabies persists. A subgroup was also formed in 2015 for Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela, coordinated by PAHO-PANAFTOSA, the Andean Health Organization, and the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization. Annual meetings in the region review and discuss rabies research and control efforts, with an international committee comprising members from Brazil, Canada, Mexico, and the USA. In the Asia-Pacific region, supported by the European Commission-funded Highly Pathogenic Emerging Diseases project established in 2010, a tripartite workshop operationalized the One Health concept in member countries. WHO, the Institut Pasteur, and the University of Lausanne organized the first international training course on rabies surveillance and control for Asian countries in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 2015. This course aimed to establish networks of local champions in seven countries. Similar courses were previously held in Senegal (2013), Cambodia (2015), and Cameroon (2016), with the next planned for Tehran, Iran, in October 2017, targeting countries in the Middle East and Central Asia. In Europe, the WHO Rabies Bulletin Europe, created in 1977, is hosted by the WHO Collaborating Centre for Rabies Surveillance and Research at the Friedrich-Loeffler Institute in Germany. This database is utilized by over 40 European countries to report confirmed rabies cases in humans and animals quarterly. The European Union's rabies subgroup, part of the task force on eradicating animal diseases, includes private and governmental experts who assess and recommend co-financed oral rabies vaccination (ORV) campaigns in member and neighboring non-member states. Since 2008, the European Union Reference Laboratory for Rabies in Nancy, France, has organized annual meetings of European national rabies laboratories to standardize diagnostic techniques. The Middle East and Eastern Europe Rabies Expert Bureau (MEEREB), an inter-regional network established in 2010, comprises representatives from Central Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. These regions are enzootic for rabies, and the network works to improve rabies control and prevention at local, regional, and global levels. In 2015, MEEREB members met in Lyon, France, to review the rabies situation and discuss the application of the One Health approach to combat rabies. Globally, rabies is a priority for the tripartite collaboration of WHO, FAO, and OIE. Efforts focus on eliminating dog-mediated rabies through multi-sectoral leadership and collaboration. Research priorities include improving the delivery of rabies interventions, developing cost-effective vaccines, and enhancing surveillance and diagnostic capabilities, particularly in low-resource endemic settings.
